newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Analysts worry over possible Cockerill merger.
newsitem.headline: Analysts worry over possible Cockerill merger.

text.p: Belgian steel group Cockerill, whose shares were suspended on Wednesday, may announce a merger with another steel firm, analysts said, adding that this could spell financial trouble for Cockerill.
Belgian steel analysts said a merger could be with either loss-making Forges de Cabecq or privately-owned Usines Gustave Boel (UGB), two small Belgian steel makers.

Some said that Cockerill may be announcing a merger with UGB in order to prevent Dutch steel group Hoogovens from making a bid for UGB. "It could be a preemptive strike as UGB in talks with Hoogovens," said Patrick Geldermans at Kredietbank.
"A merger won't be very positive for Cockerill because the UGB plant doesn't produce as good quality as Cockerill; this would be too much work for Cockerill," he added.

But steel analyst Isabelle Defranne at brokerage Mignon, Hanart, Declerck said: "The negotiations with Hoogovens and UGB seem to have gone so far that I don't think Cockerill will be able to merge with UGB".

She said a merger with Clabecq was more probable, considering the pressure the Walloon region's government, which holds a majority stake in Cockerill, was putting on the firm for it to merge with another Walloon steel maker.
"This would be a political decision because financially buying Clabeq would be negative and cost a lot of money for Cockerill," she added.
But the European Commission's decision to rule within weeks on a proposed 1.5 billion Belgian francs capital injection to rescue Clabecq, could reduce the negative impact of Clabecq on Cockerill.

"In the long term it would maker sense to have a merger. Cockerill is rather efficient in terms of technology but the problem is that the other two (Clabecq and UGB) are not really as efficient," BBL steel analyst Olivier Heuschling said.
He added that a merger without any real change would have a very negative effect on Cockerill, but was confident Cockerill would make positive changes were a deal to emerge.
"There's a will within Cockerill to be more profitable as they've shown by announcing plans to lay off 2,000 Cockerill workers," he said.
